tagline: Paul's urgent letter to churches tempted to add circumcision and the law of Moses to faith in Christ, and his defense of the freedom the gospel gives.
overview:
Galatians is the angriest and most personal of Paul's letters. Soon after he had planted churches in Galatia, a region of what is now central Turkey, other teachers arrived and told his Gentile (non-Jewish) converts that faith in Jesus was not enough: to belong fully to God's people, they must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. Paul writes to call them back. He skips his usual thanksgiving, tells the story of his own call to show that his gospel came from Christ and not from Jerusalem, recounts a public clash with Peter at Antioch, and then argues from Scripture and from the Galatians' own experience of the Spirit that people are set right with God through faith in Christ, as Abraham was, and not by the works of the law.

The letter's last two chapters turn to what that freedom looks like. It is not license to do as one pleases. It is life led by the Spirit, which produces love, joy, peace, and the rest of the fruit Paul lists, and which bears other people's burdens. Paul ends by taking up the pen himself and boasting in nothing except the cross.

Few short books have mattered more. Galatians shaped the early church's decision that Gentiles need not become Jews to follow Jesus. It sat at the center of the Protestant Reformation, and it remains at the center of modern debates about what Paul meant by justification, faith, and the law. It is also a letter about a question every generation faces: what, if anything, must be added to Christ for someone to belong to God?
author: The letter names Paul as its author (1:1; 5:2), and almost no scholar doubts it. Galatians is one of the undisputed letters of Paul, along with Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, and Philemon. Its autobiographical detail, its fierce personal tone, and its close links to Romans in theme and vocabulary all fit the apostle. Paul writes together with "all the brothers with me" (1:2), probably his coworkers where he was writing, though none is named. As was common, he likely dictated the letter to a scribe and wrote the closing lines himself (6:11).
date:
The date depends on who the Galatians were, and that question has two main answers. The North Galatian theory holds that Paul wrote to churches in the old ethnic territory of Galatia in north-central Anatolia, around cities such as Ancyra (modern Ankara), where Celtic tribes had settled in the third century BC. Acts mentions Paul passing through "the region of Phrygia and Galatia" on his second and third missionary trips (Acts 16:6; 18:23). On this view the letter was written in the mid-50s AD, perhaps from Ephesus or Macedonia, not long before Romans, which treats many of the same themes more calmly. This was the dominant view in the early church and among many nineteenth-century scholars, including J. B. Lightfoot.

The South Galatian theory, argued influentially by William Ramsay, holds that Paul wrote to the churches of Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe, which lay in the southern part of the Roman province of Galatia and which Paul founded on his first missionary trip (Acts 13-14). Many scholars today favor this view. It allows either a mid-50s date or a much earlier one. Some who hold it date the letter to the late 40s, before the Jerusalem council of Acts 15 (about AD 49), which would make Galatians Paul's earliest surviving letter. They point out that Paul never mentions the council's decision that Gentiles need not be circumcised, which would have settled the argument, and they identify the Jerusalem visit of Galatians 2:1-10 with the famine-relief visit of Acts 11:30. Others identify Galatians 2 with the council itself and date the letter after it. Each reconstruction has real strengths, and the letter's message does not depend on settling the question.
setting:
Galatia had been a Roman province since 25 BC, a large territory running from the Celtic tribal lands in the north down to cities in the south that had been planted or refounded as Roman colonies. The churches Paul addressed were made up mostly of Gentiles who had turned from pagan gods (4:8), perhaps with some Jewish believers among them.

After Paul left, other teachers came. Paul never names them. He speaks of people who are "troubling you" (1:7) and of "those who are agitating you" (5:12), and scholars often call them the agitators or the teachers. They were almost certainly Jewish believers in Jesus who held that Gentile converts must be circumcised (5:2-3; 6:12-13) and observe the law of Moses, including its calendar of holy days (4:10). Their case was not foolish. Circumcision was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham (Genesis 17), Jesus was Israel's Messiah, and it seemed natural that those who joined Israel's Messiah should take up Israel's covenant sign. They may also have claimed the backing of the Jerusalem church and suggested that Paul had watered down the message to make it easier for Gentiles. The same question was troubling the church at Antioch (2:11-14; Acts 15:1).
purpose: Paul writes to stop the Galatian churches from accepting circumcision and the law as a condition of full membership in God's people. To do that he defends his apostleship and his gospel as coming directly from Christ (chapters 1-2), argues from Scripture that the blessing promised to Abraham comes to Jews and Gentiles alike through faith in Christ and the gift of the Spirit (chapters 3-4), and shows that freedom from the law is not freedom to sin but freedom to serve one another in love by the Spirit (chapters 5-6). Behind the argument is a pastoral fear: that the Galatians, having begun by the Spirit, will try to finish by human effort (3:3), and that Christ will then be of no value to them (5:2).
story: Galatians belongs to the period of the church's life told in Acts 13-19, when the gospel moved from Jewish communities into the Gentile world and the church had to decide on what terms Gentiles belonged. The story behind it reaches back to Abraham, to whom God promised that all nations would be blessed in him (Genesis 12:3), and to the covenant of circumcision (Genesis 17) and the law given at Sinai 430 years later (3:17). Paul reads the whole history as a single plan: the promise came first, the law was a temporary guardian until Christ came, and now in Christ the promise to Abraham reaches the nations. Romans takes up many of the same themes at greater length a few years later.
christ: Galatians is about Christ from its first sentence, where he "gave Himself for our sins to rescue us from the present evil age" (1:4). Paul's whole life has been reordered by the moment God revealed his Son to him (1:16). His most personal confession is here: "I have been crucified with Christ, and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me" (2:20). Christ is the one offspring of Abraham in whom the promises are fulfilled (3:16), the one who redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (3:13), and the Son whom God sent, born of a woman and born under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons (4:4-5). The cross stands at the center of the letter and at its end, where Paul says he will boast in nothing else (6:14).
reading:
Galatians is a real letter written in a crisis: abrupt, sarcastic in places, full of feeling. Read it at one sitting to feel its urgency. Chapters 1-2 are narrative that works as argument, and chapters 3-4 are dense scriptural reasoning best read with the Old Testament passages open.

Its central terms are debated. The Reformation reading, classically set out by Martin Luther, who lectured on Galatians and prized it highly, understands justification as God's declaring a sinner righteous by grace through faith alone, and the works of the law as any attempt to earn God's favor by obedience. The new perspective on Paul, associated with E. P. Sanders's study of first-century Judaism, James D. G. Dunn (who gave the view its name), and N. T. Wright, argues that the Judaism of Paul's day was a religion of grace and covenant, not of earning salvation. On this reading the works of the law are especially the practices that marked Jews off from Gentiles (circumcision, food laws, Sabbath), and justification concerns who belongs to God's family as well as how a sinner is made right with God. Defenders of the Reformation reading answer that Paul's argument still rests on human inability and on grace as a free gift, and many interpreters combine elements of both. Scholars also debate whether the Greek phrase pistis Christou means faith in Christ or Christ's own faithfulness. Every side agrees that Galatians sets people right with God through Christ, not through circumcision or the law.

Two misreadings are worth avoiding. The letter is not an attack on Jews or on the Old Testament, which Paul quotes as God's word throughout; his opponents were fellow believers in Jesus. And its freedom is not permission for self-indulgence, which Paul rules out (5:13).

structure.title: Greeting and rebuke
structure.summary: Paul greets the churches without a thanksgiving and expresses astonishment that they are turning to a different gospel, which is no gospel at all.

structure.title: Paul's gospel came from Christ
structure.summary: Paul tells how he received his gospel by revelation, how the Jerusalem leaders recognized it, and how he opposed Peter at Antioch. The section ends with a statement of justification by faith in Christ.

structure.title: The argument from Scripture and experience
structure.summary: The Galatians received the Spirit by faith. Abraham was counted righteous by faith, the law came later and could not cancel the promise, and in Christ believers are God's children and Abraham's heirs. Paul appeals to their shared history and to the story of Hagar and Sarah.

structure.title: Freedom and life in the Spirit
structure.summary: Paul warns against circumcision, calls the Galatians to use their freedom to serve one another in love, contrasts the works of the flesh with the fruit of the Spirit, and describes how a Spirit-led community treats one another.

structure.title: Closing in Paul's own hand
structure.summary: Paul exposes the agitators' motives, boasts only in the cross, and declares that what counts is a new creation.

themes.title: One gospel
themes.body: Paul insists there is only one gospel, the message of Christ crucified and risen, and that it cannot be supplemented. Adding circumcision as a condition of belonging does not strengthen the gospel; it turns it into something else. His fierce language (1:8-9) shows how much he thought was at stake.

themes.title: Justification by faith
themes.body: A person is justified, set right with God and counted among his people, through faith in Christ and not by the works of the law (2:16). Paul grounds this in Abraham, who "believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness" (3:6). How exactly to understand justification and the works of the law is debated between the Reformation reading and the new perspective, but the letter plainly makes Christ, not the law, the basis of standing before God.

themes.title: The law's place in God's story
themes.body: Paul does not call the law evil. It came 430 years after the promise to Abraham and could not cancel it (3:17). It was added because of transgressions and served as a guardian until Christ came (3:19, 24). Now that Christ has come, believers are no longer under that guardian. The letter's question is not whether the law is good but what time it is in God's plan.

themes.title: The Spirit and freedom
themes.body: The Galatians received the Spirit by hearing with faith, not by keeping the law (3:2). The Spirit makes them children who cry "Abba, Father" (4:6), and the Spirit, not the law, is the power for a holy life. Freedom in Christ is freedom from slavery, whether to pagan gods or to the law as a means of standing with God, and freedom for loving service.

themes.title: One people in Christ
themes.body: Because all who belong to Christ are Abraham's offspring, the divisions that once defined people no longer decide who belongs: "There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus" (3:28). The clash at Antioch (2:11-14) shows that for Paul the gospel is at stake when believers refuse to eat together.

keyChapters.why: Paul's astonishment at a different gospel and the story of his call, which establishes that his message came by revelation from Christ.
The Jerusalem meeting, the confrontation with Peter at Antioch, and the letter's central statement of justification by faith in Christ.
The argument from Abraham, the curse of the law borne by Christ, the law as a guardian, and the unity of all believers in Christ.
God sends his Son and his Spirit so that believers become sons and heirs; Paul's pastoral plea and the allegory of Hagar and Sarah.
Freedom in Christ, the warning against circumcision, and the works of the flesh set against the fruit of the Spirit.

parts.body:
Galatians is a letter. Paul wrote it to a group of churches in Galatia, a Roman province in the middle of what is now Turkey. It has 6 chapters and can be read aloud in about twenty minutes.

It is the most urgent of Paul's letters. In almost every other letter he begins by thanking God for the people he is writing to. Here he does not. Straight after his greeting he writes, “I am amazed how quickly you are deserting the One who called you by the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel” (1:6).

What had happened? Paul had told the people of Galatia about Jesus, and many of them, who had worshipped the gods of their cities, had turned to the God of Israel. They were Gentiles, people who were not Jewish. After Paul left, other teachers came. They were Jewish believers in Jesus, as Paul was. They told the new believers that trusting Christ was a good start, but that to belong fully to God's people the men must be circumcised and everyone must keep the law of Moses. Many in Galatia were ready to agree.

Paul says no. Not because the law was bad. He calls it God's law and quotes it again and again. He says no because adding anything to Christ as the price of belonging turns the good news into something else. A person is set right with God, he says, “by faith in Jesus Christ” (2:16), and Gentiles who trust Christ already belong to Abraham's family, with nothing added.

The letter does three things. Paul tells his own story, to show that his message came from Christ himself (chapters 1 and 2). He argues from the Scriptures and from what the Galatians had seen with their own eyes (chapters 3 and 4). And he shows what freedom in Christ looks like in daily life: not doing as you please, but serving one another in love by the Spirit (chapters 5 and 6).

Some of the best-known lines in the Bible are here: “I have been crucified with Christ, and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me” (2:20); “you are all one in Christ Jesus” (3:28); “the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness” (5:22). They come from a short, fierce letter written by a man who was afraid of losing people he loved.

The letter names its writer twice. It opens, “Paul, an apostle” (1:1), and later he says, “I, Paul, tell you” (5:2). Almost no scholar of any kind doubts that Paul wrote it. It is one of the letters whose authorship is not in question, together with Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians and Philemon. Its personal story, its strong feeling, and its close links to Romans all sound like the Paul of those letters.

Paul writes with “all the brothers with me” (1:2), most likely the fellow workers who were with him when he wrote. He names none of them.

At the end he picks up the pen himself. “See what large letters I am using to write to you with my own hand” (6:11). In Paul's world most letters were written down by a trained scribe, and the sender often added the last lines in his own hand, rather like a signature. Most think Paul did that here. Why his letters were large is not known. Some think his eyesight was poor, some that his hands were hurt, and some that he was simply writing big for emphasis, the way we might use bold type.

Who was Paul? He tells the Galatians himself. He was a Jew, and a strict one: “I was advancing in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries and was extremely zealous for the traditions of my fathers” (1:14). He had tried to destroy the church. Then God “was pleased to reveal His Son in me so that I might preach Him among the Gentiles” (1:15-16). The letter is written by a man who had once been sure he was defending God against the followers of Jesus, and who now gave his life to telling Gentiles about him. That is part of why it burns.

parts.h: Who were the Galatians? North or south
parts.body:
Paul writes “To the churches of Galatia” (1:2). But ‘Galatia’ could mean two different places, and readers have long asked which one Paul meant.

The name first belonged to a people. In the 200s BC, Celtic tribes from Europe crossed into Asia Minor and settled in the high country of the north, around the town of Ancyra, which is modern Ankara. Greeks called them Galatians. In 25 BC Rome made the region a province and named it Galatia, with Ancyra as its chief city. But the Roman province was much bigger than the old tribal land. It reached far to the south, and took in towns such as Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe.

So there are two main answers.

The north Galatian view holds that Paul wrote to churches in the old tribal land in the north, around Ancyra. Acts twice says that Paul passed through “the region of Phrygia and Galatia” (Acts 16:6; see also Acts 18:23), and on this view he started churches there on those trips. This was the common view of the early church, and many scholars of the 1800s held it. On this view the letter was written in the middle 50s.

The south Galatian view holds that Paul wrote to the churches he started in the southern towns of the province, which Acts describes in some detail (Acts 13 and 14). Those who hold it point out that Paul usually uses the Roman names of provinces, that Acts tells us much about these southern churches and nothing certain about churches in the north, and that Barnabas, whom Paul names three times in the letter (2:1, 9, 13), travelled with him in the south but not on the later trips. Many scholars today hold this view. It allows the letter to be dated either early, in the late 40s, or later, in the 50s.

These notes do not choose. The question matters for working out when Paul wrote, and the next part takes that up. It does not change what the letter says. On either view, the Galatians were Gentiles who had turned from the gods of their cities (4:8) to the living God, and who were now being told that this was not enough.

Galatians does not give a date. The date has to be worked out, and it depends on two questions: who the Galatians were (the part above), and how Paul's own story in chapters 1 and 2 fits with the story Luke tells in Acts.

Paul says that after he met Christ he went to Arabia and back to Damascus, and “Only after three years did I go up to Jerusalem to confer with Cephas” (1:18). Cephas is Peter's name in Aramaic. Then: “Fourteen years later I went up again to Jerusalem, accompanied by Barnabas” (2:1). On that visit the leaders in Jerusalem agreed that Titus, a Greek, did not have to be circumcised.

Which visit in Acts is that? Readers answer in three ways, as the notes on Acts 11 and Acts 15 already set out. Many think Galatians 2 is Paul's side of the meeting in Acts 15, often called the Jerusalem council, which most date in the late 40s, about AD 48 to 50. The question there was the same one: must Gentile believers be circumcised? Others think Galatians 2 is the earlier famine visit of Acts 11, when Barnabas and Paul brought gifts to Jerusalem. On that view Galatians was written before the council, which would explain why Paul never mentions the council's letter, even though it would have helped his case. A third view sees Galatians 2 as a private meeting of its own.

Put the two questions together and there are two main dates. On one, Galatians was written in the late 40s, to the southern churches, before the council, which would make it perhaps the earliest of Paul's letters that we have. On the other, it was written in the early or middle 50s, after the council, from Ephesus or Macedonia, not long before Romans. Romans, written about AD 57, takes up many of the same questions in a calmer voice, and some take the closeness of the two letters as a sign that they were written near each other.

These notes do not choose. As with every date in Paul's life, the years rest on a few fixed points and a good deal of careful guessing. The word ‘about’ matters. What does not change is the setting: a young church, a sharp question, and an apostle who believed that the answer would decide whether the gospel stayed good news.

parts.h: What had gone wrong in Galatia
parts.body:
Paul never names the teachers who came after him. He speaks of “some people” who “are troubling you” (1:7), and of “those who are agitating you” (5:12). So we know them only through his letter, and we should be careful to describe them fairly.

What the letter shows is this. They were Jewish believers in Jesus. They taught that Gentile believers must be circumcised (5:2-3; 6:12-13), and that they should keep the law of Moses, including its holy days (4:10). They may have said that Paul had made the message too easy, leaving out parts of it to please Gentiles (1:10), and that the true leaders were in Jerusalem.

Their case was not foolish, and it is worth hearing it the way they would have put it. God gave circumcision to Abraham as the sign of his covenant, and he said it was to be “an everlasting covenant” (Genesis 17:13). Jesus was Israel's Messiah. The Scriptures were Israel's Scriptures. It seemed natural that anyone joining Israel's Messiah should take up Israel's covenant sign and keep Israel's law, as Gentiles who became Jews had always done. They were not trying to add a burden for its own sake. They believed they were being faithful to God's word.

Paul's answer is that this way of thinking, however sincere, makes Christ not enough. If a Gentile must also be circumcised in order to belong, then belonging rests partly on Christ and partly on something else. As he puts it, “if righteousness comes through the law, Christ died for nothing” (2:21). And it splits the church into two kinds of believers, those who have the mark and those who do not.

The same question troubled the church in Antioch, where Peter, Barnabas and Paul all lived and ate with Gentile believers (2:11-14; Acts 15:1). So this was not a quarrel between Christians and Jews. It was a quarrel among Jewish believers in Jesus about how Gentiles come into God's family. Paul, a Jew, was on one side of it. Other Jews, believers in the same Lord, were on the other. And the leaders in Jerusalem, Paul says, agreed with him (2:6-9).

Galatians falls into three parts, with a short opening and a closing in Paul's own hand.

The opening (1:1-10). Paul greets the churches, names Christ “who gave Himself for our sins” (1:4), and then, where a thanksgiving would go, he rebukes them. Any other gospel is no gospel.

Chapters 1 and 2: Paul's story. Paul shows that his message came straight from Christ, not from other people. He tells how he persecuted the church, how God called him, how he met Peter only briefly years later, and how the leaders in Jerusalem accepted his work among the Gentiles. Then he tells of a hard day in Antioch, when he challenged Peter in front of everyone. The part ends with Paul's statement of the heart of the matter: a person is set right with God by faith in Christ, not by works of the law (2:15-21).

Chapters 3 and 4: the argument. Paul asks the Galatians how they received the Spirit: by keeping the law, or by hearing and believing (3:2)? He goes back to Abraham, who “believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (3:6). He shows that God's promise to Abraham came long before the law, and that the law could not cancel it. He calls the law a guardian, a servant who looked after a child until he grew up. Now that Christ has come, all who belong to him are God's children and Abraham's heirs. He pleads with them as a mother in labour. And he ends with a picture drawn from Abraham's two sons.

Chapters 5 and 6: freedom lived out. Paul says, “It is for freedom that Christ has set us free” (5:1). Then he says what freedom is for: “serve one another in love” (5:13). He sets the works of the flesh beside the fruit of the Spirit, and tells the churches to restore those who fall, carry each other's burdens, and not grow tired of doing good.

The closing (6:11-18). Paul takes the pen, names the teachers' motives, and boasts in one thing only: “the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (6:14).

Look for the words that come back: gospel, grace, faith, law, promise, Spirit, flesh, freedom, slavery, sons, heirs. Paul is not repeating himself by accident. Each one carries part of the argument.

One gospel. Paul insists that there is only one good news: Christ crucified and risen, God's own rescue of sinners. It cannot be improved by adding something to it. He says it so strongly that he calls down a curse on anyone, even himself or an angel, who preaches another (1:8-9). That is hard to hear, and the note on 1:6-10 says more about it. But it shows how much Paul thought was at stake.

Grace, and the cross as God's own act. Salvation in Galatians starts with God. Christ “gave Himself for our sins to rescue us from the present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father” (1:4). God called Paul “by His grace” (1:15). Christ “redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (3:13). God “sent His Son” and “sent the Spirit of His Son into our hearts” (4:4, 6). The church confesses this, not as one view among others but as the faith: people are saved by the grace of God, through the cross, as God's own act.

Faith. A person is set right with God “by faith in Jesus Christ” (2:16), as Abraham was by trusting God's promise. Faith is not a new kind of good work. It is receiving what God gives.

The Spirit. Paul's strongest evidence is what had already happened among the Galatians. They received the Spirit when they heard and believed, before anyone told them to be circumcised (3:2-5). The Spirit makes them God's children, who cry “Abba, Father” (4:6), and grows in them the fruit of a new life (5:22-23).

Freedom. Paul uses the words slave and free again and again. Christ has set people free from the guardian of the law, from the false gods they once served (4:8), and from the need to earn a place in God's family. But freedom is not doing whatever you want. Paul says, “do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh. Rather, serve one another in love” (5:13).

One family. The question in Galatia was who belongs, and on what terms. Paul's answer is that in Christ Jews and Gentiles belong together as one people, children of Abraham, eating at one table. “There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (3:28).

Paul argues in Galatians from the Scriptures of Israel, the same Scriptures his opponents used. He does not set the Old Testament aside. He reads it as God's word and says it was pointing to Christ all along.

His key text is Genesis 15:6: “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (3:6). Abraham was counted righteous by trusting God, years before he was circumcised and centuries before the law was given at Sinai. And God promised him, “All nations will be blessed through you” (3:8; Genesis 12:3). For Paul this means the gospel was announced to Abraham in advance: God always meant to bring the nations into his family.

In chapter 3 Paul quotes several texts in a row. He quotes Deuteronomy 27:26, on the curse for not keeping the law (3:10). He quotes Habakkuk 2:4, “The righteous will live by faith” (3:11). He quotes Leviticus 18:5, on the one who does these things living by them (3:12). And he quotes Deuteronomy 21:23, on the one hung on a tree (3:13). The chapter notes take each one in its own setting.

In chapter 4 he tells the story of Abraham's two sons, Ishmael and Isaac, from Genesis 16 and 21, and quotes Isaiah 54:1, a song of joy for a barren woman (4:27). In chapter 5 he sums up the whole law in the words of Leviticus 19:18: “Love your neighbor as yourself” (5:14). And he ends with a blessing of peace and mercy (6:16) that echoes the prayers of Israel, “Peace be upon Israel” (Psalm 125:5).

Where Paul's wording differs a little from the Old Testament in the Berean Standard Bible, it is usually because he follows the old Greek translation of the Scriptures, which was widely used in his day, while the BSB translates the Old Testament from the Hebrew. The chapter notes point this out where it happens.

One thing is plain all the way through. For Paul the law is God's good gift. He asks, “Is the law, then, opposed to the promises of God? Certainly not” (3:21). In Romans he says, “the law is holy, and the commandment is holy, righteous, and good” (Romans 7:12). His quarrel is not with the law. It is with making the law the gate into God's family, when God had already opened the gate in Christ.

parts.h: ‘Works of the law’ and ‘faith in Christ’: the readings
parts.body:
Paul says, “a man is not justified by works of the law, but by faith in Jesus Christ” (2:16). Two phrases in that sentence are read in more than one way, and the book page on Romans sets out both questions at more length.

‘Works of the law.’ The traditional reading, long taught in Protestant churches, takes it to mean everything a person does to obey God's law, done as a way to stand right with God. On this reading Paul's target is any attempt to earn God's favour, since no one keeps the law well enough to stand on his own record. Galatians 3:10 seems to say just that: those who rely on the law are under its curse, because it requires everything.

A second reading is often called the ‘new perspective’ on Paul. In 1977 the scholar E. P. Sanders argued that the Judaism of Paul's day was not a religion of earning salvation: God chose Israel by grace, and the law was the way to stay faithful within that covenant. In 1982 James Dunn gave the approach its name, and N. T. Wright and others developed it. On this reading ‘works of the law’ means above all the practices that marked Jews off from other peoples, such as circumcision, the food laws and the Sabbath, the very things at issue in Galatia. Paul's point is that Gentiles do not have to become Jews to belong to God's people.

Each reading has strong defenders. Those who hold the second say it fits the actual quarrel in Galatia, over circumcision and over who may eat with whom. Their critics answer that Paul also speaks of the whole law and of a curse on all who fall short, and that grace shuts out every kind of human achievement. Many readers take something from both. These notes set out both and do not settle it.

‘Faith in Christ’ or ‘the faithfulness of Christ’. The Greek phrase behind ‘faith in Jesus Christ’ is pistis Christou, word for word ‘faith of Christ’. It can mean our trust placed in Christ, as most English Bibles take it, the BSB among them. Or it can mean Christ's own faithfulness, his trust in his Father and his obedience all the way to the cross. The American scholar Richard Hays argued for the second in 1983, and many have followed him. Others answer that Paul plainly speaks of our believing in the same verse: “we, too, have believed in Christ Jesus” (2:16). These notes do not choose. On either reading Paul teaches both things: Christ was faithful for us, and we are to trust him.

All these readings agree on what matters most. No one is set right with God by circumcision or by the law, and Gentiles who trust Christ belong to God's people without becoming Jews.

Galatians is short, but it has shaped the church far beyond its size.

The question it answers, whether Gentiles must keep the law of Moses to belong to Christ, was settled in the first generation. After that, the church kept reading Galatians because of what lay under the question: how a sinner is set right with God, and what freedom in Christ means.

At the Reformation the letter became a banner. Martin Luther lectured on Galatians more than once, and a commentary from his later lectures was published in 1535. He loved the letter so much that, in a remark his friends wrote down, he called it his own epistle, to which he was betrothed, and gave it the name of his wife, Katie von Bora. For Luther, Galatians said that a troubled conscience could rest on Christ's work and not on its own.

More than a hundred years later, an English tinker named John Bunyan, who had long been tormented by fear that he could not be saved, came on an old, worn copy of Luther's commentary in English. In his book Grace Abounding (1666) he wrote that, apart from the Bible, he preferred it to all the books he had ever seen, as ‘most fit for a wounded conscience’. He went on to write The Pilgrim's Progress.

In the twentieth century, scholars began to ask again what the quarrel in Galatia was really about. The ‘new perspective’ described above came partly from reading Galatians closely, with its talk of circumcision, food and who may eat with whom. Readers still argue about how to hold the two together: the troubled conscience that Luther heard in the letter, and the divided table that Paul saw in Antioch.

Galatians 3:28 has had a long life of its own. Christians have read it in debates about slavery, about race in the church, and about men and women. The note on 3:26-29 says what all agree it means, and where churches differ.

Galatians is a sharp letter, and it has sometimes been read in ways that Paul would not recognise. So it helps to say what it is not.

It is not a letter against the Jewish people. This needs saying plainly, because it has been misused. Paul was a Jew. So were Peter, James, Barnabas and the teachers in Galatia. The quarrel was among Jewish believers in Jesus, about how Gentiles come into God's family. When Paul speaks of “the present-day Jerusalem” in his picture of Hagar and Sarah (4:25), he is making an argument about his own day with an image, and the note on 4:21-31 explains it. He is not passing a verdict on Jews then or now. The same Paul wrote of his own people, “Theirs is the adoption as sons; theirs the divine glory and the covenants” (Romans 9:4). For centuries some Christians used words from the New Testament to justify contempt for Jews. That reading is false, and this site rejects it, as the note on Acts 2:22-28 sets out.

It is not a letter against God's law. Paul quotes the law as Scripture. He says the whole law is fulfilled in love (5:14). What he opposes is making the law a condition of belonging to Christ.

It is not a licence to do as you please. Paul's freedom is freedom to love. He warns that those who live by the works of the flesh “will not inherit the kingdom of God” (5:21).

It is not a call to contempt for other Christians. Paul is fierce toward teachers who were, in his judgment, changing the gospel itself. But the same letter tells believers to restore one who falls “with a spirit of gentleness” (6:1), warns against “biting and devouring one another” (5:15), and calls conceit and envy works of the flesh. It gives no one permission to treat every disagreement as a battle for the gospel.

And it is not a letter about any nation. When Paul says that in Christ there is “neither Jew nor Greek” (3:28), he is speaking of one people of God from every people. The cross belongs to no flag. Any teaching that ties the gospel to one nation's power, or that promises wealth as the reward of faith, turns the letter upside down: Paul boasts only in the cross (6:14).

Read it in one sitting. It takes about twenty minutes. It was written to be read aloud to gathered churches, so read it aloud if you can, and listen for the change of voice: anger, then argument, then tenderness, then warning, then hope.

Keep the question in mind. Every chapter answers one question: must Gentile believers be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to belong fully to God's people? When a verse seems hard, ask how it helps answer that.

Read chapters 3 and 4 with your Bible open at Genesis. Paul's argument is about Abraham, and it is easier to follow when you have read Genesis 12, 15, 16, 17 and 21 for yourself.

Notice the feeling. Paul is not writing a cool essay. He is afraid for people he loves. “My children, for whom I am again in the pains of childbirth until Christ is formed in you” (4:19). His sharp words come from that fear, and they sit beside his gentleness.

Do not stop at chapter 4. Some readers treat Galatians as only an argument about how a person is saved. But the last two chapters show what that salvation is for: a people who walk by the Spirit, carry one another's burdens, and do good to everyone.

Let the letter read you. It asks what you are adding to Christ, quietly, as the price of belonging: a background, a way of worship, a list of rules, a political side. It asks who you would rather not eat with. And it tells of a Son who “loved me and gave Himself up for me” (2:20).

The notes on each chapter go through it passage by passage in plain words.

hard.line: ‘Let him be under a curse.’ Why Paul speaks so fiercely about another gospel, and why this gives no one licence to curse those they disagree with.
Paul opposes Peter at Antioch. What Peter did, why Paul said it to his face, and why the story is told without contempt for Peter.
‘Not by works of the law, but by faith in Jesus Christ.’ The two readings of ‘works of the law’, and ‘faith in’ or ‘faithfulness of’ Christ.
‘Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us.’ What the curse was, and what the cross did.
‘Seed’, not ‘seeds’. How Paul reads the promise to Abraham as pointing to Christ.
‘All of you who were baptized into Christ.’ What churches agree on about baptism, and where they differ.
‘Neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female.’ What all agree it says about standing in Christ, and where churches differ on what follows.
Hagar and Sarah. What Paul's picture means, why it is no verdict on Hagar or on the Jewish people, and the misuse that must be rejected.
‘You have fallen away from grace.’ What Paul warns against, and how Christians read it alongside God's promise to keep his people.
Paul's harshest sentence. Why he wrote it, and why it is not a pattern for how believers speak.
‘The Israel of God.’ Whether Paul means the whole church, Jewish believers in Jesus, or Israel as a people.

words.line: Greek euangelion, good news. Paul says there is only one, and it came “by revelation from Jesus Christ” (1:12).
Greek charis, God's free gift and the goodwill behind it. God called Paul “by His grace” (1:15). To add the law as a condition is to set it aside (2:21).
Greek dikaioō, to set in the right, to declare in the right, a word from the law court. A person is justified “by faith in Jesus Christ” (2:16).
Deeds the law of Moses requires. Read as any effort to earn God's favour, or above all as the marks of Jewish identity such as circumcision. See the part above.
Greek pistis, trust, and also faithfulness. Abraham “believed God” (3:6). Faith receives what God gives; it is not a new work to earn it.
Greek nomos. In Galatians usually the law God gave through Moses at Sinai, 430 years after the promise to Abraham (3:17). God's good gift, but not the gate into his family.
God's word to Abraham that the nations would be blessed through him. The law “does not revoke” it (3:17). In Christ it reaches the Gentiles.
The sign of God's covenant with Abraham (Genesis 17). The teachers in Galatia said Gentile believers must receive it. Paul says, “neither circumcision nor uncircumcision means anything” (6:15).
Greek paidagōgos, a household slave who looked after a boy until he grew up. Paul's picture of the law's work “to lead us to Christ” (3:24).
God's own Spirit, given when the Galatians heard and believed (3:2). The Spirit makes believers God's children and grows the fruit of a new life (5:22).
Greek sarx. In Galatians not the body as such, but human nature turned in on itself, and human effort as a way to stand before God (3:3; 5:19).
Greek eleutheria. Freedom from slavery to the law's guardianship and to false gods, given for love: “serve one another in love” (5:13).
The Aramaic word for father, used by Jesus (Mark 14:36). The Spirit leads Gentile believers to pray it too (4:6).

timeline.what: The two dates most often proposed for the death and rising of Jesus in Jerusalem.
Paul, a zealous Pharisee who persecuted the church, meets the risen Christ near Damascus. He goes to Arabia and back to Damascus (1:15-17).
Paul goes up to Jerusalem and stays fifteen days with Peter, seeing also James, the Lord's brother (1:18-19).
Paul works in the regions of Syria and Cilicia, where his home town of Tarsus lay (1:21; Acts 9:30).
Barnabas and Paul start churches in Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe, in the southern part of the province of Galatia (Acts 13 and 14).
Paul goes up to Jerusalem with Barnabas and Titus. The leaders give him the right hand of fellowship (2:1-10). Which visit in Acts this is, is debated.
The meeting in Jerusalem of Acts 15: Gentile believers need not be circumcised. Many think Galatians 2 tells of it; others think Galatians came first.
Peter draws back from eating with Gentile believers at Antioch, and Paul opposes him to his face (2:11-14).
Paul writes Galatians. The earlier date goes with the south Galatian view; the later date with either view.
Paul writes Romans, which takes up many of the same questions more calmly.
A commentary from Martin Luther's lectures on Galatians is published. He called it the letter he loved most.
John Bunyan, in Grace Abounding, praises Luther's Galatians as most fit for a wounded conscience.

map.title: Galatia, north and south, and the places of Paul's story

places.name: Ancyra
places.line: Today's Ankara, the chief city of the old Celtic land of Galatia and of the Roman province. On the north Galatian view, Paul wrote to churches in this region, which Acts mentions only in passing (Acts 16:6; 18:23).

places.name: Pisidian Antioch
places.line: A Roman colony in the south of the province, where Paul preached in the synagogue (Acts 13:14-52). On the south Galatian view, one of the churches this letter went to.

places.name: Iconium
places.line: Today's Konya, in the south of the province. Paul and Barnabas started a church here (Acts 14:1-7). On the south Galatian view, one of the churches this letter went to.

places.name: Lystra
places.line: Where Paul was stoned and left for dead (Acts 14:19). If the letter went to the south, the Galatians may have seen the scars he calls “the marks of Jesus” (6:17).

places.name: Derbe
places.line: The farthest town of Paul's first trip in the south of the province (Acts 14:20-21). Its exact site is not certain.

places.name: Tarsus
places.line: Paul's home town, in Cilicia. After his first visit to Jerusalem he went to “the regions of Syria and Cilicia” (1:21).

places.name: Antioch in Syria
places.line: The great city where believers were first called Christians, and where Jewish and Gentile believers ate together. Here Paul opposed Peter to his face (2:11-14).

places.name: Damascus
places.line: Near here Paul met the risen Christ. After a time in Arabia he “later returned to Damascus” (1:17).

places.name: Jerusalem
places.line: Where Paul stayed fifteen days with Peter (1:18), and where, fourteen years later, the leaders gave him “the right hand of fellowship” (2:9).

teaching.mapNote: Two answers to ‘Which Galatia?’ The old Celtic land around Ancyra in the north, or the southern towns of the Roman province: Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe, marked without names on the drawing and listed below. Arabia (1:17) is not marked; the letter names no town there.
